newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Blair says EU summit gave UK all it wanted.
newsitem.headline: Blair says EU summit gave UK all it wanted.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Wednesday all his demands were met at the European Union summit, with Britain's border controls guaranteed and a deal secured to keep NATO at the heart of Europe's defence.
Blair told a news conference he had also won assurances on quota-hopping designed to protect Britain's fishermen which he intended to unveil later in the day in parliament in London.

Saying this was a result of his new, positive approach to Europe, Blair said: "We were fighting on the ground we should be fighting on, protecting our interests in the way we should be protecting our interests, not causing a fuss for the sake of it.

"As a result of that, I think that we secured every single objective we came here for," he said after a marathon summit which took until the early hours of Wednesday to agree a watered-down treaty to ready the bloc for new members.
Blair dismissed suggestions the summit conclusions were minimalist and would need to be revised later, saying the treaty made it clear enlargement was now a "major objective".

Blair also hailed the fact a deal on Monday on jobs and growth designed to heal a rift between France and Germany over progress towards monetary union and a single currency had focussed on flexible labour markets rather than spending plans.

"The summit as a whole has focussed in a very, very important way on the issue of jobs, economic reform, the focus being on education, skills, flexible labour markets rather than old-style state intervention and regulation," said Blair.

Blair has claimed the drive for jobs was a British initiative and has pledged to push forward efforts to cut red-tape and boost employment when London takes over the rotating EU presidency next January.

Citing the deal on borders, which he said had eluded the former Conservative government for 18 years, and the employment deal, opposed in principle by former prime minister John Major, Blair said he had "reshaped Britain's place in Europe".
Other leaders were complimentary. Outgoing Irish premier John Bruton said: "It's fair to say the contribution from Britain was very positive right across the range of issues."
But despite Blair's clear triumphs on borders, jobs and defence, some question marks remained.
Spanish officials dismissed Blair's claim of a deal on quota-hopping -- foreign, mainly Spanish, fishermen who have bought up British fishing quotas.
First reactions from groups representing fishermen in Britain were also negative, with claims there was nothing new.

But Blair said the European Commission had established a clear link between the quotas and the nationality of the fishing licence -- jargon for forcing quota fishers to land a significant part of their catch in British ports.
The real test will come when Blair reads out the Commission's letter in the lower House of Commons.
But Blair is expected to get a warm reception from his own Labour party members of parliament while the Conservatives are in the middle of a divisive hunt for a leader to replace Major.
